entries.title: Russia releases imprisoned U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard following Trump's request
entries.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin says he has freed an American, Stephen Hubbard, from a Russian prison following a request from President Trump.
entries.content:
Russia releases imprisoned U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard following Trump's request

Trump envoy Steve Witkoff visits Russia as Trump administration hopes to end war

Russian President Vladimir Putin says he has freed an American, Stephen Hubbard, from a Russian prison following a request from President Trump.

The announcement came as talks got underway between Putin and White House envoy Steve Witkoff focused on U.S. efforts to end the war in Ukraine.

The 74-year-old Stephen Hubbard of Michigan was detained by Russian forces in eastern Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced — after a closed trial in 2024 — to nearly seven years in prison, for serving as a mercenary in the Ukrainian army.

As talks with Witkoff got underway in Russia's former imperial capital of Saint Petersburg, Putin announced Hubbard had been released and was already at Pulkovo Airport, in St. Petersburg.

Prior to the talks, Trump said he had asked Putin to release Hubbard, whom the U.S. had formally designated wrongfully detained under the Biden administration.

Hubbard's release comes as Trump has lifted some sanctions on Moscow — and openly criticized Ukraine — amid U.S. efforts to negotiate an end to the war.

entries.title: 2025 policing trend: Fewer serious crimes, more minor arrests
entries.summary: Arrests for more minor offenses, including vagrancy, rose in the U.S., even as violent crime rates dropped to historic lows, according to an analysis from criminal justice reform advocacy group FWD.us
entries.content:
2025 policing trend: Fewer serious crimes, more minor arrests

Arrests for low-level crimes, including vagrancy and drug possession, rose in the U.S. from 2024 to 2025 even as rates of violent crime including homicide plummeted to historic national lows, according to a new analysis of federal data from the criminal justice and immigration reforms advocacy group FWD.us.

Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us, spoke to NPR ahead of the report's release on Wednesday.

"This increase signals a really troubling return to some of the extreme law and order policies that defined the American criminal justice system during the 80s and the 90s," Towns said, referring to the era's tough-on-crime policies, including mandatory minimum prison sentences, that led to a massive rise in incarceration in the U.S. for decades.

The report analyzes publicly available FBI and immigration arrest data and does not include details of whether charges were dropped or if people served any time in jail or prison.

Still, Towns said, "An arrest has life-changing consequences for the person involved and for their family. It can mean days or months in jail. It can mean a lost job. It can mean missed rent or a missed mortgage payment," and can mean families separated, she said.

A representative for the FBI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on this analysis.

The findings

Four states, California, Hawaii, Nevada and Arizona, accounted for over half the increase in vagrancy arrests, according to the report. The legal definition of vagrancy is "roaming from place to place without a permanent job, home, or material resources." In practice, it is disproportionately enforced against people experiencing homelessness.

FWD.us found arrests for vagrancy were up 44% (22,769 in 2024 to 32,728 in 2025).

Two demographic groups made up the majority of arrests: Asian Americans, as well as Native Hawaiian and other Pacific Islanders. Although AANHPI people make up only about 7% of the US population, they accounted for 17% of the increase in vagrancy arrests, largely in Hawaii, according to FWD.us

Marijuana possession arrests went up 6%, mainly in Southern states that have not yet legalized the drug. The report showed there were 190,182 arrests in 2024 and 201,273 a year later.

There was a stark racial disparity between those arrested for marijuana possession: Black people accounted for 83% of the national increase in marijuana arrests in 2025 and nearly half of all cannabis arrests were of Black people (45%).

Arrests for possession of drugs other than marijuana rose marginally between 2024 to 2025. The report found a national increase of 3% in arrests or 508,087 in 2024 and 523,520 in 2025.

This increase appears to be tied to the unraveling of policies that decriminalized drug possession in some states.

Voters in California (which saw the biggest jump in arrests for drug possession) back in 2024 voted to roll back a measure that had reclassified drug possession from a felony to a misdemeanor. Proposition 36, approved by voters, increased criminal penalties for repeat thieves and drug users. FWD.us says drug possession arrests rose by over 14,000 in a single year following its passage.

That same year Oregon similarly reinstated a policy that made simple drug possession a criminal offense again. That resulted in a 39% increase (2,205) in non-marijuana drug possession arrests.

The report also highlights the vast increase (188%) in arrests for immigration violations in that time — a trend NPR has previously covered. In 2024, there were a reported 109,936 immigration violation arrests. A year later, in 2025, those arrests totaled 316,304.

Why is this happening now?

FWD.us ties the increases, in part, to changes at the federal level.

The data reviewed by FWD.us covers the first full year of President Trump's second term in office. In that time the administration leaned on a tough-on-crime message.

It supercharged its deportation efforts, arresting hundreds of thousands nationwide — many of whom had no criminal convictions. Millions of federal dollars have also been sent to local police through the 287(g) program, which allows local police to make immigration arrests.

FWD believes federal deployments of immigration officers and the National Guard may have also led to increased policing and subsequently more arrests.

In summer 2025, Trump claimed American cities including Washington, D.C., were suffering from a "crime emergency" — despite data showing violent crime in the city were at a record low in 2024. He sent hundreds of National Guard troops to the city.

FWD.us found that arrests in D.C. for marijuana possession "more than doubled" following the Trump administration's deployment of National Guard into the city.

Vagrancy arrests may also be tied to actions by the Supreme Court, according to FWD's report. Two years ago, the judges ruled that cities can ban people from sleeping and camping in public places. The ruling allowed Oregon and dozens of other Western localities to limit where individuals living in cars, parks and other encampments stayed.

Insha Rahman, president and director of the criminal justice reform nonprofit Vera Institute, says there are still "incredibly positive trends" showing crime across the board is down.

Adult arrests for drug crimes peaked in 2006 at about 1.7 million, more than 2.5 times the number recorded in 1980.

And has continued a downward trend.

Rahman says this decrease "speaks to the resilience of states and localities that have continued to double down and invest in what works." Vera was not involved in the FWD.us report.

That includes investing in treatment and diversion programs that offer assistance to people struggling with addiction, community violence intervention programs, youth services, counseling and alternative response programs.

entries.title: Expecting a baby? 5 tips to help you prepare for pregnancy costs
entries.summary: The cost of having a baby is difficult to predict. The amount families pay varies widely. Here are five tips to help you prepare for the often unexpected costs of pregnancy and giving birth.
entries.content:
As Grace Griffin and her husband were welcoming their long-awaited baby — a daughter — Griffin found herself worried about looming medical bills and unsure whether the family could pay for the care needed.

"This whole experience has me wondering (keeping me up at night, actually): Can we ever afford to have another child?"

— Grace Griffin, Calumet, Michigan

Grace and Daniel Griffin, both 26, knew money would be tight once they had their first child. So, even before the Calumet, Mich., couple tried to conceive, they began crunching the numbers to figure out the cost of pregnancy.

"We wanted to save up enough to pay for those medical bills right away, if possible," Grace said.

But the cost estimator that she found linked to her UnitedHealthcare student plan asked for medical billing codes for each procedure that Grace was likely to receive. That's information she didn't have.

So, she kept digging until she found the Summary of Benefits and Coverage information on the health plan's website, which estimated out-of-pocket costs for a routine pregnancy and delivery at about $2,700.

"We thought, 'OK, that's doable,'" she said. "We should be able to save up that much and pay for that out of pocket."

But as the expenses piled up, it was clear the estimate wasn't even close.

Early in the pregnancy, Grace met her $500 deductible, the out-of-pocket cost she had to pay before insurance pitched in. Her plan also required her to pay 20% coinsurance for in-network care. This meant that for every $100 billed for things like routine blood work and other needed care, she was on the hook for $20.

"When I started getting lab work is when we started realizing expenses would add up quickly," Grace said. Routine blood tests to check iron levels or for gestational diabetes were a couple of hundred dollars every visit, she said.

In June, after what Grace described as a routine pregnancy and delivery, the couple welcomed their daughter. Then the Griffins received an "explanation of benefits" notice that showed the hospital charged about $18,000 for the delivery, with the family on the hook for a sizable portion.

"I thought, 'Oh no, it's going to be a lot,'" she said. "Much more than we budgeted for."

She was right.

In early October, Grace said, her family's out-of-pocket expenses had totaled more than $9,000, over three times the general estimate published by her insurer for pregnancy-related costs.

Meanwhile, Grace and Daniel are scrambling to cover their bills.

For years, federal lawmakers have tried to remedy this issue, said Sabrina Corlette, a research professor and co-director of Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms. To make healthcare costs more transparent and accessible to patients, Congress required insurers to provide consumers with an individualized "advanced explanation of benefits" estimating what scheduled care would cost them. The rule, part of the 2020 No Surprises Act, was due to take effect on Jan. 1, 2022, but federal regulators have yet to make that happen, despite ongoing pressure from members of Congress.

"So, it's basically 4 1/2 years since this was supposed to be available, and I think it's a source of a lot of frustration for a lot of folks," Corlette said. "People have a right under the law to know these things."

Meanwhile, she said, another change is pending. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, long-standing maternity billing codes that bundle much of pregnancy care will be replaced with more detailed coding for prenatal care, labor, delivery and postpartum care.

The change could make it easier to see what individual services cost, but Corlette said it's not yet clear whether the change will make it easier for people trying to stick to a budget.

"I could see where it might be advantageous to the provider," she said. "But I'm not sure I'm seeing benefits to the patient."

Until out-of-pocket maternity expenses get easier to estimate, here are some tips to help you budget for the cost of pregnancy.

1. Enroll your baby before the clock runs out

Ensuring your newborn has health coverage is one of the first paperwork responsibilities that parents face in the whirlwind of bringing a baby home.

Birth creates what's known as a special enrollment opportunity, meaning you don't have to wait until the annual open-enrollment period to sign up a newborn.

Many employer health plans require parents to request enrollment within 30 days of birth. Marketplace plans — for those who buy their own insurance rather than get it from an employer or the government — generally allow 60 days. Wait too long, and your baby may be left uninsured until the following year.

Michelle Critzer of Ventura, Calif., learned that lesson the hard way. She works as a sales rep and is the mother of a toddler and a newborn. Her second son, Hudson, was born in February, and Critzer missed the enrollment deadline for him. Ever since, she has been asking her insurer to make an exception — so far, without success.

"The way they set hard must-do's within 30 days of having a baby is actually insanity," she said.

The family was able to enroll Hudson in a health plan through Critzer's husband's workplace, which has a 60-day enrollment window. But that coverage is not nearly as robust as Critzer's insurance, she said. Still, she's grateful to have Hudson insured while she continues pressing her own plan to enroll him.

2. Ask about must-know numbers, like your MOOP

Budgeting for a pregnancy often begins with a tally of the expected expenses. The deductible is the amount you'll pay before much of your insurance coverage kicks in.

After that, you'll likely face copayments — fixed fees paid each time you receive service, regardless of the size of the bill.

Coinsurance is another expected expense, but as Grace discovered, it can be especially tricky to estimate. Coinsurance requires the patient to pay a percentage of the cost for each service received.

MOOP, which stands for "maximum out-of-pocket" expense, is another must-know number. Your plan's MOOP is the ceiling on what you'll pay each year for covered, in-network services (care that your health plan has contracted to pay at negotiated, lower rates).

Think of it as doomsday prepping. Some people get comfort from knowing and planning for the worst-case scenario. Under the Affordable Care Act, in 2026 the amount a person has to pay out of pocket for in-network care is capped at $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family. Your plan might set a lower maximum, but once your spending reaches your plan's limit, insurance pays 100% of all further in-network costs for that year.

One complication to be aware of: If your pregnancy overlaps two plan years, the tally of your out-of-pocket expenses resets to zero at the beginning of the second year, and you could find yourself maxing out your out-of-pocket expenses two years in a row.

Some plans have two MOOPs, one for in-network services and another for out-of-network benefits. Insurance plans usually track those expenses separately, and the out-of-network MOOP can be double the in-network limit. That's more incentive to meticulously seek out in-network care.

As a family, the Griffins had an $18,000 MOOP, and Grace's individual maximum was $9,000.

3. Choose in-network care, when you can

You picked an obstetrician in your plan, but don't assume others on the care team are in-network providers.

Ask about the hospital, labs and imaging facilities your doctor's office may use. Corlette, of Georgetown's Center on Health Insurance Reforms, suggests that patients explicitly tell the doctor's office to send tests to an in-network provider.

Federal law protects patients who go to an in-network hospital or other in-network facility from out-of-network "surprise bills" issued by out-of-network providers.

4. Check every bill — and don't be afraid to file an appeal

The Affordable Care Act requires certain recommended prenatal services to be covered without any additional cost to you. Among them: prenatal visits, folic acid, anxiety and depression screening, and breastfeeding and lactation counseling and supplies.

Still, these costs sometimes get mistakenly passed on to the patient.

To protect against billing errors, Corlette suggests patients become familiar with these pregnancy-related services and then check every bill.

If your insurer refuses to pay for a covered charge, consider filing an appeal.

5. Seek help before the bills pile up

Most hospitals offer financial assistance programs. Find out whether yours will work with you, either to reduce your bill or to offer a manageable payment plan. Your doctor or other providers might also offer assistance, if you ask.

Corlette said to make sure any arrangement is formally agreed upon in advance so the account isn't unexpectedly turned over to collections.

Also investigate other assistance.

Grace Griffin qualified for Michigan's Rx Kids program, which provides eligible families in certain communities with $1,500 during pregnancy and $500 a month for the baby's first six months or year of life.

That money has helped keep the medical bills from devouring the Griffins' emergency savings.

"It takes a lot of pressure off," she said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling and journalism.

entries.title: LeBron James talks smack with Knicks fans in victorious 76ers debut
entries.summary: The Sixers got a first look at the potent lineup they put together this summer in hopes of winning their first title since 1983.
entries.content:
LeBron James talks smack with Knicks fans in victorious 76ers debut

NEW YORK — LeBron James got the business from Knicks fans still gloating and riding an emotional high from an NBA championship banner celebration.

As he stepped to the free-throw line for the Philadelphia 76ers early in Tuesday night's season opener, Knicks fans erupted toward James with chants of "We don't want you! We don't want you!"

Such a rude reception from New Yorkers to one of the city's newest residents.

The shouts of rejection came in part because there was a plausible scenario under which James would have opened the season at Madison Square Garden in a Knicks uniform.

James and his agent, Rich Paul, had said the Knicks would have been James' first choice in free agency had New York not won its first NBA championship since 1973 last season.

Knicks fans said, we're good.

The 41-year-old James got the final word as the Sixers won 106-100.

James talked smack with fans in the lower level. Yes, that was Spike Lee trying to play peacemaker.

James finished with 14 points and nine rebounds and had plenty of help in getting the W from new Sixers and holdovers. Tyrese Maxey scored 28 points, Jaylen Brown had 19, Joel Embiid had 13 points and 11 rebounds, and the Sixers ruined the Knicks' championship party.

A good night in New York totally spoiled? Not quite, according to James.

"I wouldn't say that," James said. "It was a great night for New York fans. Fifty-plus years. I was a part of that at one point where we hadn't won a major championship in Cleveland in over 50 years. The fans will never forget this moment."

James' first basket for the Sixers was not nearly as memorable. He took a feed from Embiid in the paint and went up strong for an uncontested right-handed layup.

Just two points. Just one bucket of what the Sixers expect to be many, many more over the next two seasons as the NBA's career scoring leader opened his record 24th season.

Embiid appeared to wonder during the national anthem where the Knicks' championship banner was hanging in the rafters as James sat nearby on the bench with his head bowed and hands clasped.

The banner was indeed raised in a pregame ceremony.

It's the same kind of celebration the 76ers expect James, Embiid and the rest of a stout starting lineup to deliver on opening night next season.

It's the thrill of the chase, to end a championship drought — much like he did to break that drought in Cleveland — that in part drives James to keep playing after racking up a list of accomplishments unrivaled by his peers.

Sixers hope new starting five can jell and make title run

The Sixers got a first look at the potent lineup they put together this summer in hopes of winning their first title since 1983. James and a fellow All-Star in Brown started alongside holdovers Embiid, Maxey and VJ Edgecombe.

There are some questions about how that All-Star starting four plus Edgecombe will coexist when all have been the primary ballhandlers on their respective teams in the past. Who gets the ball in crunch time? Who has to sacrifice the most? Who has the most to gain?

Watching the answers unfold in real time will be fascinating for the Sixers and their fans.

The chemistry looked strong throughout the night. James hit Brown cutting to the basket to earn the assist on the former Celtics star's first points with the Sixers. The Sixers closed the third quarter with an 11-0 run, capped by Brown's second straight 3-pointer that came at the buzzer and gave Philadelphia an 83-76 lead.

"We did that on the fly," James said.

The offseason all the way through the countdown to the Sixers' home opener Thursday against Cleveland has been a swirl of excitement in Philadelphia. James jerseys are flying off the racks. Murals of him have popped up all over the city. He drew more than 10,000 fans to a public scrimmage and preseason games were sold out. There's a fascination with his helicopter rides from the Sixers' facility in New Jersey to New York.

Even his younger teammates admitted to being a bit awestruck when they first met James.

The Sixers entered the Garden almost unrecognizable from when they played there in early May in a second-round playoff series. They lost twice in New York and the Knicks finished the sweep in Philadelphia.

The Sixers loaded up with talent and pushed the payroll so they could challenge the Knicks.

"It's certainly been fun these first few weeks," coach Nick Nurse said. "These guys have been really great."

There's not much left for James to accomplish, except win that fifth ring.

Philadelphia is waiting.

entries.title: FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service
entries.summary: Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines.
entries.content:
FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service

Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines. The Federal Aviation Administration approved the Max 10 for passenger service Tuesday, ending years of delays.

The 737 Max 10's certification represents another milestone in Boeing's efforts to restore its reputation and financial footing after years of safety, quality and production challenges. With production approved, the aircraft can now be sold to domestic and foreign carriers.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the certification followed "extensive safety reviews," including thousands of hours of test flights, and called it a major win for American manufacturing.

"To think that it took us almost 10 years to get here. We all probably had a little less gray hair 10 years ago," Duffy said during a visit to Boeing's manufacturing plant Tuesday in Everett, Washington.

The Max 10 is an important piece of the company's effort to regain ground in the narrow-body market. For airlines, the larger plane offers a way to carry more passengers on a single flight, potentially lowering costs per seat. For travelers, it could eventually mean more seats on popular routes, though the impact on fares will depend on how airlines deploy the planes and how much competition they face.

Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said during Duffy's visit that the certification "clears the path to deliver an airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation." The Max 10 will typically seat 185-210 passengers, according to Boeing, compared with 175-195 on the Max 9 and 160-180 on the Max 8.

"Today is a very, very special day. It caps years of hard work and dedication by many," Pope said. "It marks another major milestone in our recovery, and it unlocks a key to our future growth."

The company expects to begin deliveries in 2027.

The single-aisle jet was introduced at the Paris air show in 2017 to help Boeing compete with rival Airbus. But technical and regulatory hurdles repeatedly delayed certification.

Boeing's struggles have been particularly acute since two deadly crashes involving the smaller Max 8 killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 off the coast of Indonesia and in Ethiopia. In 2024, a panel flew off of an Alaska Airlines Max 9 in midair, renewing scrutiny of Boeing's manufacturing and safety practices.

The delays have held up a key part of Boeing's business. More than 30 customers worldwide have ordered 1,555 Max 10s that Boeing has yet to deliver, accounting for more than 30% of its total 737 Max backlog.

Major customers include United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and Ryanair. Alaska Airlines joined that list in January, ordering 105 Max 10s, with options for 35 more.

The Max 10 is intended to compete with Airbus's A321neo model family, which entered service in 2017. The largest A321neo can carry more passengers and fly farther without refueling than the Max 10.

Still, Boeing designed the Max 10 to carry more passengers while burning less fuel than older aircraft — a potentially attractive combination for airlines facing soaring jet fuel costs amid the U.S. war with Iran. Those rising costs have put added pressure on airlines to control expenses.

Certification means the FAA has determined that the Max 10's design meets safety standards, following engineering reviews and flight testing. But Boeing must continue to show it can consistently build the aircraft to the approved design, and each plane must be cleared before it can fly passengers.

The Max 10's certification completes the lineup of four 737 Max models. The FAA cleared the Max 7 for airline operations in August.

Pope on Tuesday described the certification of both the Max 7 and Max 10 in the same year as a sign of the company's resilience.

In the wake of the fatal Max 8 crashes, the FAA overhauled how it certifies Boeing aircraft. But over the past 18 months, the agency has gradually eased some of its restrictions on the company, increasing the limit on how many planes Boeing can produce. In July, the FAA also said Boeing could once again issue airworthiness certificates for its 737 Max and 787 planes at the end of production, allowing the company to take back some responsibility for determining whether finished aircraft are ready to fly.

entries.title: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
entries.content:
Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles following recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice, leaving civilians vulnerable.

For at least a week, the Ukrainian leader has said that his country has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. Such intelligence, he said, saves lives by allowing the public to be alerted and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles.

Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said on a visit to Norway. "So we are thankful to American side now that it works."

Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio acknowledged mutual frustration between the U.S. and Ukraine over intelligence sharing and weapons supplies but emphatically denied that the Trump administration has made any changes to previous policy on either issue.

US envoy to go to St. Petersburg

In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelenskyy sought more American and European help.

Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with the Ukrainian president in Norway's capital.

Gahr Støre said Witkoff planned to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders, exchange ideas from the Oslo meeting and share proposals from European and American colleagues.

"Today was a good day for peace," Stubb said.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow is willing to listen to new U.S. proposals about Ukraine but doesn't expect any "miracle" from Washington.

At the White House, President Donald Trump stepped up the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again.

"We want Zelenskyy to make a deal," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss."

If that doesn't happen, "I think it's going to be a very bad thing."

Zelenskyy speaks with Rubio after US support slows

The conversation with Rubio came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."

Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russian ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine.

The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations.

Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia, a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow's full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February.

Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio.

"I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media.

Rubio, who arrived Tuesday in India on an official trip, denied that the U.S. is withholding assistance from Ukraine.

"Nothing has changed," he told reporters.

The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said.

"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said.

Europe tries to make up for waning US supplies

European countries, worried about Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made.

European countries and European Union institutions have allocated 237 billion euros ($266 billion) to support Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros ($129 billion) from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace.

"Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now," Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms "because Europe has been supporting Ukraine," Kallas said.

Russian attacks cause power outages in 12 Ukrainian regions

Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said.

Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.

On Tuesday morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The dead included the driver of a shuttle bus that was hit. The bus transports people from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery.

Two more people were killed in a Russian attack Tuesday on warehouses on the outskirts of Dnipro in central Ukraine, authorities said.

National grid operator Ukrenergo reported power outages in 12 regions of Ukraine following the Russian attacks.

The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement that its forces carried out drone strikes on logistics centers, port infrastructure and three cargo ships in the port of Reni in the Odesa region. It said that another bulk carrier was hit at sea on its way to Odesa.

Meanwhile, air defenses intercepted 136 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.

entries.title: France announces nightly curfews 'for as long as necessary' in Paris and other cities
entries.summary: Fresh curfews were being imposed across the city centers of Paris and Lyon on Tuesday after the first quiet night since France's most destructive rioting in years.
entries.content:
France announces nightly curfews 'for as long as necessary' in Paris and other cities

PARIS — Fresh curfews were being imposed across the city centers of Paris and Lyon on Tuesday after the first quiet night since France's most destructive rioting in years, as Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said a "massive" security operation was planned for new protests Saturday.

Paris police said the curfew in two designated zones — around Place de la République and the Les Halles shopping district — had restored "public peace" overnight and would remain in place "for as long as necessary." The curfew zones leave out other areas hit on Saturday, including the Champs-Elysées and the area around the Saint-Lazare train station and parts of the Rue de Turbigo in central Paris, where protesters set up barricades and lit fires.

In Lyon, one of France's largest cities, authorities also renewed a curfew in the city center from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., saying no disturbances had been recorded overnight.

Marseille, France's second-largest city, imposed a curfew for unaccompanied minors starting Tuesday night. Lecornu said the targeted curfews "helped keep last night calm."

Student unions and groups from the " yellow vest " movement, whose protests over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, have called for another day of protests Saturday.

Soldiers from Sentinelle, the anti-terrorism operation that has patrolled French cities since the 2015 Islamic State group attacks, will take over guarding sensitive sites to free up more police officers and gendarmes for crowd control, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers Tuesday.

"The deployment (of police forces) for next Saturday will be massive," Lecornu told the National Assembly, France's lower house of parliament, without giving figures.

Suspect held over Limoges city hall fire

Police on Tuesday arrested a suspect in the arson attack that charred the historic city hall in Limoges, in central France, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said, adding that the person was being held in police custody and may not have acted alone.

French media reported that the suspect was close to radical environmentalist movements and was on a watchlist of people considered potential threats to national security. Darmanin declined to comment on the suspect's profile, but said far-left groups appeared to have organized to attack symbols of the state throughout France.

Footage of the 143-year-old building in flames, its bell tower collapsing, spread widely online over the weekend. U.S. Vice President JD Vance shared it on X, blaming the unrest on immigration and writing, "I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn." President Donald Trump, who also relayed the video, said migrants had "taken over France."

French officials have instead blamed the violence on far-left groups and opportunistic looters. At least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France on Saturday clashed with police, set cars on fire and stormed public buildings, during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.

On Sunday evening, small groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities.

In Paris on Monday night, a police helicopter circled over Place de la République overnight, a central point in the weekend clashes, sweeping the square with a searchlight to check that the curfew was being respected.

Early Tuesday morning, workers used a crane to remove a giant fluorescent yellow vest draped over the statue at the center of the square, then used pressure washers to blast graffiti off the monument.

Louise Belanger, a volunteer who came to help with the cleanup, said she still could not apprehend the level of violence. "Normally when you are 20 you should be optimistic, you should be starting to build something (...) If you are only anger and violence, what are you going to do? This is sad for everybody in society," she said.

Courts promise 'extremely firm' response

Speaking in Lille, northern France, Darmanin said 149 people had been jailed nationwide as of Tuesday at noon. According to the Justice Ministry, of the roughly 2,400 people arrested since Saturday, more than 800 have been sent before prosecutors, most of whom were either put on trial immediately or ordered to appear at a later hearing.

In Paris alone, about 300 people have been sent before prosecutors following the Oct. 17 protests, the city prosecutor's office said in a statement.

Darmanin said he had asked prosecutors to appeal any sentence they considered too lenient. "People with no criminal record ending up in prison for property crimes is extremely rare, if not unheard of," he said, arguing that the French justice system will be "extremely firm."

In Lille, he said, three men aged 20 to 25 with no criminal record were each sentenced to 10 months in prison and jailed immediately for looting a video game store in the city's old town.

The National Assembly is launching an inquiry into the Oct. 17 violence and the authorities' policing strategy, its speaker, Yaël Braun-Pivet, said, with findings expected "by the end of the year."

Protests continued Tuesday on a smaller scale. Some 400 people, mostly high school and university students, marched in the western city of Rennes, and about 750 in Lyon, under pouring rain.

entries.title: United Nations report highlights significant increase in U.S. climate pollution
entries.summary: The U.S. is the only major economy where planet-warming pollution dramatically increased last year. The United Nations warns the planet is on track for catastrophic warming.
entries.content:
United Nations report highlights significant increase in U.S. climate pollution

Countries are not doing enough to cut emissions that cause climate change, according to a new report from United Nations scientists. And the United States is a big part of the problem.

The U.S. sticks out as the only major economy where planet-warming pollution increased dramatically last year, the report notes.

It finds that last year, the U.S. was tied with Russia as the G20 countries with the most per capita emissions of carbon dioxide and other planet-warning gases. China emits significantly more total greenhouse gases each year than the U.S., but has more than four times the population.

Overall, global emissions were basically the same last year as they were the previous year.

U.S. emissions grew because of increased electricity demand, as well as Trump administration policies that support the burning of fossil fuels. The Trump administration has ordered coal-fired power plants in the U.S. to stay open longer than planned, rolled back fuel-efficiency standards for vehicles and ended tax credits for solar and wind projects.

Those policies have made the U.S. an outlier when it comes to escalating greenhouse gas emissions, says Inger Andersen, the executive director of the U.N. Environment Programme.

"Right now, everybody is scrambling a little bit regarding energy security," Andersen says, pointing to global oil and gas disruptions stemming from the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

Despite the geopolitical upheaval, "several G20 members have shown sustained emissions reduction," she notes.

That includes the European Union, which has invested heavily in energy-efficient appliances and renewable electricity sources such as wind and solar, partly in reaction to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The U.S. is pulling out of U.N. climate work

The Trump administration has withdrawn from the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, and is working to remove the U.S. from all U.N. climate work, arguing the international system imposes unfair burdens on Americans. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency now says greenhouse gases do not pose a threat to human health and welfare, reversing its previous position.

The new report includes a statement from the U.S. government, saying the U.S. "does not endorse or agree with its analysis or conclusions, and has not provided comments to this report." The U.S. State Department did not respond to NPR's questions.

The new report, which is compiled annually by an international group of scientists, comes less than a month before global climate talks kick off in Turkey. World leaders will gather to discuss how to speed investments in clean energy and how to pay for the costs of dealing with climate change. The Trump administration will not participate in those talks.

Still, whether or not American leaders formally participate in international climate efforts, the effects of America's reliance on oil, gas and coal are being felt around the world, the U.N. warns. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, trapping extra heat that warms the entire planet. The effects of all that pollution are felt globally.

The Earth is about 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5 degrees Celsius) warmer on average than it was in the mid-1800s, according to the World Meteorological Organization. That warming is driving widespread disasters, from deadly heat waves and floods to more intense storms and wildfires.

"All countries, especially the big emitters, must do more," says U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. "Every fraction of a degree matters."

The Earth is on track for 5 degrees Fahrenheit of warming this century

Right now, the planet is on track for upwards of 5 degrees Fahrenheit (2.8 degrees Celsius) of warming this century, which would cause catastrophic impacts, such as massive sea level rise and the mass extinction of plants and animals, the report warns.

The U.N. Paris Climate agreement sets a goal of limiting warming to well below 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit (2 degrees Celsius), in the hopes of avoiding such cataclysms.

This is the first year the annual report has acknowledged that even lower targets are now out of reach. However, it finds it is still possible to keep warming below 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, if global greenhouse gas emissions fall by about 25% in the next decade.

But countries are currently lagging far behind that goal.

Under the Paris agreement, about two thirds of countries have submitted formal, up-to-date plans for cutting their greenhouse gas emissions. If they all follow through on those plans, it would reduce emissions by about 15% in the next decade — far less than the 25% needed.

entries.title: Some on DOJ's 20,000 "likely" noncitizen list in Calif. appear to be U.S.-born
entries.summary: Election officials in Los Angeles County say their preliminary analysis of the federal government's list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote in California shows the list is "unreliable."
entries.content:
Some on DOJ's 20,000 "likely" noncitizen list in Calif. appear to be U.S.-born

The Department of Justice is demanding California take the unprecedented step of segregating ballots associated with 20,000 people the department says are "likely" noncitizens. But an initial review by local officials suggests the list is "unreliable" and that some people on it had indicated in records they were born in the U.S. and therefore may be citizens.

The new details come from court filings submitted Tuesday by the state of California and local officials, in response to a lawsuit filed by the federal government attempting to compel the state to investigate the thousands of people before their votes are counted. The state says doing what the DOJ requests would be unfeasible this close to the election and would likely break federal and state election laws.

"At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt," the state wrote in Tuesday's filing. "At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election."

The saga began in earnest last week when the Justice Department delivered a thumb drive to Los Angeles County that contained the list of roughly 20,000 people who investigators at the Department of Homeland Security say are "likely noncitizens" and registered to vote somewhere in California.

Initially, county officials declined to open the list, citing the security threat of inserting a thumb drive of unknown origin into a government computer. The next day, the DOJ emailed a spreadsheet with the same list.

Out of the 20,000 names on the list, only 7,035 had addresses in Los Angeles County and some were duplicates, according to a separate Tuesday court filing by Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan.

In declarations to the court, Los Angeles County officials wrote that they took a sample of 200 people to get a sense of how reliable the federal government's data might be.

"The review is preliminary and quality control is continuing, but it indicates that the October List is unreliable," wrote Monica Flores, Los Angeles County Assistant Registrar-Recorder.

Of the voters where birthplace was "meaningfully reported," Flores wrote, "38.9% indicate that they were born in the United States, which is strong evidence of citizenship."

It's unclear how many people that is in total or the specifics of which records listed place of birth. NPR has reached out to the LA county clerk's office for clarity on the numbers listed in the court filings but by Tuesday evening had not yet received a response.

The California Secretary of State's website asks for "place of birth" when people register to vote online, although the field is not mandatory.

Except for extremely narrow exceptions, anyone born in the U.S. automatically receives citizenship.

Of the 200 records the county staff reviewed, 112 were associated with people whose registrations are canceled or inactive. The filing also said around 70% of the people sampled had no voting history.

The Trump administration has generally defended its methodology for finding noncitizen voters, without fully ever publicly explaining it. Other numbers federal officials, including President Trump, have recently released on the issue of noncitizen voting have been shown to be inaccurate in other cases.

Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter acknowledged there could be some errors in the federal government's list of 20,000 names in a Monday press conference. "There may be some names on there who it turns out ultimately are citizens, we're not perfect," McCotter said. "And that's why we've asked California to cooperate with us."

In response to questions about LA County's initial analysis, DOJ deputy press secretary Kiersten Pels said in a statement, "California cannot facilitate the violation of federal law." The statement continued, "We notified California that noncitizens are likely registered to vote, and we asked the state to independently verify the citizenship of any ballots cast by people on a list that we provided. It refused to do so. Federal law doesn't permit this willful blindness."

On Monday, the DOJ also announced criminal charges against 28 people on the list provided to the state. But even in those cases, it seems some of those charged may have registered without understanding it was illegal.

Kamlesh Shah, 68, told Sacramento TV station KCRA 3 he thought he was able to vote because he had a Real ID.

"I'm feeling very depressed, very full of anxiety. I'm disabled. I've got so much problems in my heart, my condition, so it's going to give me more stress," Shah told KCRA 3. "I'm very upset. I'm trying to get an attorney, hopefully I can have the charges dismissed."

All 28 of the people charged Monday were legal permanent residents, also known as green-card holders. Research has shown that in the rare cases when noncitizens vote, it is often green-card holders who misunderstand the rules as opposed to intentional fraud.
